report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **well-supported by strong evidence**. Add-on cannabidiol (CBD, marketed as Epidiolex) significantly reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children and young adults with Dravet syndrome compared with placebo.

The pivotal evidence comes from a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Devinsky et al., NEJM 2017) of 120 children/young adults with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome, which found that adjunctive CBD (20 mg/kg/day) significantly reduced convulsive seizure frequency over 14 weeks compared to placebo, though with more adverse events (diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, elevated liver enzymes) (nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618). A subsequent dose-ranging randomized trial (JAMA Neurology, 2020) confirmed that both a 10 mg/kg/day and 20 mg/kg/day dose significantly reduced convulsive seizures versus placebo, with the higher dose showing greater efficacy but more side effects (jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458). Long-term open-label extension data (Epilepsia, 2018) further showed sustained, clinically meaningful seizure reductions with an acceptable long-term safety profile (onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/epi.14628). This body of evidence led the FDA to approve Epidiolex specifically for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome (and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex) (drugs.com/history/epidiolex.html).

Network meta-analyses comparing CBD, stiripentol, and fenfluramine as add-on therapies for Dravet syndrome also support CBD's efficacy, though all agents carry tolerability trade-offs, and CBD is not uniquely superior—choice may depend on individual patient factors.

**Bottom line:** The claim is accurate—CBD as an add-on therapy reduces convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome, based on high-quality randomized controlled trial evidence, though it is associated with notable adverse effects requiring monitoring.
